### Describe the feature Tempo's pitch is that the payment lane stays fast even when the general lane is busy. But I can't find anywhere that actually measures it. We report TPS and gas, not whether payments land fast while the general lane is full. That's the real question behind tempoxyz/tempo#4155: 8k TPS tells you nothing about payment UX under load. Most of the pieces are already there: * [mix.yml]() already runs payments next to DEX/MPP traffic * `tx-latency` already records [tempo_tx_landing_latency_seconds](), just not split by lane * the payload builder already splits payment vs general for gas/count, just not latency
So it's mostly a reporting layer: tag latency by lane, then aggregate into an SLO Proposed steps: 1. Add a `payment` / `non_payment` label to the latency histogram, using the same [is_payment]() check the builder uses 2. Report payment p50/p95/p99, goodput under a configurable target, and SLO miss rate in the `bench-e2e` summary 3. Add a preset that floods the general lane (DEX swaps / MPP ops) while a steady payment stream runs Implementation notes: * `tx-latency` mixes clock sources. Pending uses local `SystemTime::now()`, landing uses the block header timestamp. Fine for rough numbers, but skew will wreck a sub-second SLO, so worth normalizing. * classifying by lane means `tx-latency` has to keep the full tx envelopes (it only keeps hashes today) and know the active hardfork. Open question: should the SLO numbers live in the `bench-e2e` summary JSON first, with Grafana/ClickHouse as a follow-up? ### Additional context Not the same as [benchmarkoor-replay]() / [execution-payloads-benchmarks](), which measure aggregate throughput by replaying payloads. This is the per-lane latency angle they don't cover. Stays in bench/sidecar tooling, no protocol changes.

## Summary

`EvmPrecompileStorageProvider` in `tempo/crates/precompiles/src/storage/evm.rs` stores `is_static` from the call context but never checks it in any of the three state-mutating methods: `sstore`, `tstore`, and `emit_event`.

If a Tempo precompile is invoked via `STATICCALL`, all three operations silently succeed and mutate EVM state. No error is returned, no gas is refunded — the mutation just happens.

## Affected methods

- `sstore` — writes persistent storage
- `tstore` — writes transient storage  
- `emit_event` — emits a log

All three are state-modifying operations. None of them guard against `self.is_static`.

## Spec

This is a direct violation of [EIP-214](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-214) (STATICCALL), which specifies:

> Any attempts to make state-changing operations inside an execution instance with `STATIC` set to `true` will instead throw an exception. These operations include `CREATE`, `CREATE2`, `LOG0`–`LOG4`, `SSTORE`, and `SELFDESTRUCT`.

`TSTORE` is also covered under EIP-1153, which applies the same static-context restriction.

The Yellow Paper formalises the `STATIC` execution environment flag introduced by EIP-214; once set, any state modification must result in an exceptional halt.

## Impact

A contract can invoke a Tempo precompile via `STATICCALL` and cause persistent or transient storage writes and log emissions that the caller's execution context assumes cannot happen. This breaks the core invariant that `STATICCALL` provides to callers: that no state has changed after the call returns.
payload.title: sstore/tstore/emit_event: is_static flag never checked in EvmPrecompileStorageProvider

payload.body:
## Summary

`EvmPrecompileStorageProvider::set_code` in `tempo/crates/precompiles/src/storage/evm.rs` has two related issues:

### 1. Silent code overwrites are possible

`set_code` does not guard against writing bytecode to an address that already has code. If the account already has a non-empty code hash, `set_code_and_hash_slow` is called unconditionally, silently replacing the existing bytecode. No error is returned.

Today this is safe only because the single production caller (the `TokenFactory`) performs its own `already_deployed` pre-check before calling `set_code`. But that is a caller-side convention, not an invariant enforced by `set_code` itself. Any future caller that omits the check will silently overwrite live contract code.

### 2. TIP20 detection relies on an implicit heuristic

The comment on the CREATE gas block reads:
```
// TIP-1016: charge TIP20 deployments as CREATE.
if self.amsterdam_eip8037_enabled && was_empty { ... }
```

`set_code` does not actually know whether the deployment is a TIP20 token — it infers this from `was_empty` (i.e. "the account had no prior state"). These two conditions happen to be equivalent today because the factory always deploys to fresh addresses, but that is coincidental rather than enforced.

If a future precompile calls `set_code` on an empty non-TIP20 address (e.g. for account abstraction or keychain initialization), it would silently be charged the full 500,000 gas CREATE cost, which is incorrect and difficult to trace back to this code path.

### High-level directions

- Add an explicit overwrite guard inside `set_code` that returns an error if the account already has a non-empty code hash, making the invariant impossible to violate from any call site.
- Replace the `was_empty` heuristic with an explicit check that confirms the target address has a supported B-20 token prefix (the infrastructure for this already exists in `TokenVariant::is_b20_address`), so the TIP-1016 CREATE charges only fire for actual TIP20 deployments.
payload.title: set_code: missing overwrite guard and implicit TIP20 detection

### Describe the change

After confirming in earlier research that eth_getTransactionCount only reflects the protocol nonce (nonce_key =
  0), I started using the NonceManager precompile's getNonce(address, uint256) (selector 0x89535803, at 0x4e4F…0000)
   to read 2D nonce lanes.

  But getNonce requires a specific nonceKey as a parameter — it doesn't enumerate. Since NonceManager.nonces is a
  mapping(address => mapping(uint256 => uint64)), Solidity doesn't expose key enumeration, and the precompile's
  INonce interface exposes only this one view function.

  So the practical situation for an external caller seems to be:

  - Protocol nonce — queryable via eth_getTransactionCount.
  - 2D nonce lane k — queryable via getNonce(addr, k), only if the caller already knows k.
  - Set of 2D lanes used by an address — not queryable on-chain directly. Seems to require scanning
  NonceIncremented(address indexed account, uint256 indexed nonceKey, uint64 newNonce) event logs.
  - Expiring nonce (TIP-1009, k = U256::MAX) — not counted anywhere on-chain (hash-based replay, no counter).
  getNonce(addr, U256::MAX) always returns 0.

  So even combining eth_getTransactionCount + getNonce(addr, k) cannot compute a full "transactions sent by this
  account" count without also indexing logs or maintaining an off-chain index.

  Questions:

  1. Is this understanding correct — that a complete count cannot be computed purely from on-chain view calls, and
  that NonceIncremented event scanning (+ off-chain tracking for expiring nonces) is the intended path?
  2. Is there a plan for an aggregation-friendly RPC (e.g. tempo_listNonceKeys(address) or a total-count helper) so
  third-party tooling doesn't need to scan historical logs for every query?

  Thanks!

### Describe the bug

Affected crate: tempo-transaction-pool (`crates/transaction-pool/src/tempo_pool.rs`).

`evict_invalidated_transactions()` can push the same tx hash twice when one pending AA transaction matches both Check 4 (blacklist addition) and Check 5 (whitelist removal) in the same maintenance scan.

payload.author: decofe
payload.body:
## Summary

New validators joining the network should be placed in the `Secondary` peer group instead of immediately being tracked as primary peers.

## Motivation

Commonware's p2p layer supports `TrackedPeers` with distinct `primary` and `secondary` sets ([p2p/src/lib.rs#L234-L258](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/main/p2p/src/lib.rs#L234)). Secondary peers:

- Are accepted for inbound connections
- Receive `Recipients::All` broadcast traffic on established connections
- Are visible in `PeerSetUpdate` notifications
- Are **not** dialed outbound (saving connection overhead)

The [reshare example](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/main/examples/reshare/src/dkg/actor.rs#L305-L317) demonstrates the intended pattern:

```rust
// Primary = dealers (drive the DKG round/running consensus)
// Secondary = current players + next-epoch players (give time to sync)
//
// Overlapping keys are deduplicated as primary
self.manager
    .track(
        epoch.get(),
        TrackedPeers::new(
            dealers.clone(),
            Set::from_iter_dedup(players.iter().chain(next_players.iter()).cloned()),
        ),
    )
    .await;
```

Currently, Tempo's `PeerManager` (`crates/commonware-node/src/peer_manager/actor.rs`) tracks all validators — including next-epoch players read from the DKG outcome — as a flat `ordered::Map<PublicKey, Address>` passed to `oracle.track()`, which places them all as primary peers. This means we eagerly dial validators that may not yet be participating in consensus.

## Changes

1. **`peer_manager/actor.rs`**: Change `track_or_overwrite` and `refresh_peers` to distinguish between:
   - **Primary**: current epoch's active players/dealers (those currently participating in consensus)
   - **Secondary**: next-epoch players (`onchain_outcome.next_players()`) and any newly registered validators not yet in the active set

   Use `TrackedPeers::new(primary, secondary)` when calling `oracle.track()` instead of the current flat peer map.

2. **`validators.rs`**: May need to return richer data (e.g., which validators are current vs next-epoch) so the peer manager can split them. Currently `read_active_and_known_peers_at_block_hash` merges everything into one map.

3. **`read_peer_set_if_boundary`**: Currently unions `players()` and `next_players()` into one flat `Set`. Should pass them separately so the caller can assign primary/secondary.

## Benefits

- Avoids unnecessary outbound dials to validators that haven't started participating yet
- Gives new validators time to sync and establish inbound connections before being relied upon
- Aligns with commonware's recommended peer group pattern
- Reduces connection churn during validator set transitions
payload.title: feat(peer-manager): place newly incoming validators in Secondary peer group

After [PR #3554](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/pull/3554) we set `ForwardingPolicy::Disabled` and ignore `Relay::Plan` in the `broadcast` implementation.

Commonware's simplex engine now supports forwarding certified blocks to peers who missed them — either to all non-voters (`Silent`) or just the next view's leader (`NextLeader`). The `Plan` enum distinguishes initial `Propose` broadcasts from targeted `Forward { round, peers }` rebroadcasts.

We should:
1. Evaluate whether enabling forwarding improves liveness under real-world conditions (missed proposals, slow validators)
2. If so, implement plan-aware relay logic that handles `Forward` by sending only to the specified peers
3. Pick the right policy (`Silent` vs `NextLeader`) based on our validator set size and network profile
payload.title: feat(consensus): evaluate simplex ForwardingPolicy and Relay::Plan

After [PR #3554](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/pull/3554) we use the new `Logs` API from commonware, but we still collect all dealer logs at once and call `finalize`/`observe` immediately — missing the incremental verification benefit.

We should call `Logs::record()` as each dealer log is finalized in a block, and `Logs::pre_verify()` periodically (e.g. after each batch of new logs), so that signature verification is amortized over the epoch rather than done all at once at the boundary block.

This matters more as the validator set grows.

### Summary
On Moderato testnet, Tempo TIP-20 native USD precompiles are callable from deployed contracts, but contract deployment from Foundry against the public RPC shows two surprising behaviors:

1. `forge script` calling TIP-20 precompiles inside the script VM hits `OpcodeNotFound`
2. large contract creates on-chain can consume the full gas cap and fail even when local Foundry deployment gas is much lower

### What I verified
TIP-20 precompiles are not wallet-only:
- direct RPC `cast call` to `pathUSD` / `AlphaUSD` / `BetaUSD` / `ThetaUSD` works
- a deployed Solidity probe contract can call `balanceOf(...)` on all four
- a deployed Solidity probe contract can call `approve(...)` on `pathUSD`, and the allowance is stored on-chain

Example successful contract-originated approve:
- token: `0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000000`
- tx: `0x3458b929d74331dc1ffe99446cdd5c3505d93af017fb2f4355520844e130f9a7`

### Unexpected behavior
For `PredictionMarket` deployment on Moderato:
```bash
forge create src/PredictionMarket.sol:PredictionMarket \
  --broadcast \
  --gas-limit 20000000 \
  --rpc-url https://rpc.moderato.tempo.xyz \
  --private-key <funded-key>
```

Receipt:
- tx: `0x5f38ff9fc3c2d29436d098c74aa5b040159da19a5c31b99bfd801dcb838ed314`
- status: `0`
- gasUsed: `20000000`

- reported contractAddress: `0x6b821802e2cB86d3082EA47342b6d49D3618D62d`
- `cast code` at that address returns `0x`

Local Foundry gas report for the same contract says deployment cost is about `5,216,990` gas, so the live failure is unexpectedly far above local expectations.

### Question
Is there any known Moderato behavior around:
- contract creation gas accounting when fees are paid in TIP-20 stables
- precompile behavior inside Foundry-style script/simulation paths
- limits or caveats for deploying larger contracts through the public RPC

If there is a recommended deployment method for large contracts on Moderato, that would help.

## Summary

When a server's 402 challenge includes `feePayer: true` in `methodDetails`, `tempo request` sends `feeToken: 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000` in the `eth_estimateGas` RPC call. Tempo's node rejects this with `TIP20 token error: InvalidToken(InvalidToken)`, preventing the channel open transaction from being built.

## Reproduction

```bash
# Server issues challenge with feePayer: true
# (mpp.lasso.sh is a live MPP gateway)
tempo request -vvv -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"eth_blockNumber","params":[],"id":1}' \
  https://mpp.lasso.sh/fastest/ethereum
```

In the trace output, the `eth_estimateGas` call shows:
```json
{
  "feeToken": "0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000",
  ...
}
```

Tempo responds: `{"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"TIP20 token error: InvalidToken(InvalidToken)"}}`

## Expected Behavior

The CLI should use the payment currency address (available in the challenge's `request.currency` field) as the `feeToken` for gas estimation, even when `feePayer: true`. The mppx TypeScript SDK does this correctly — it passes `feeToken: currency` to `prepareTransactionRequest` alongside `feePayer: true`.

The sender doesn't sign over `feeToken` when sponsored (per spec), but gas estimation still needs a valid token to compute costs.

## Context

payload.body:
## Summary

`eth_estimateGas` returns ~305k gas for a TIP-20 transfer when the request uses the `calls` array format, vs ~50k when using `to`+`data` format. Since viem always converts to `calls` format for Tempo TXs, every gas estimate from the wallet is inflated ~6x.

## Repro

```bash
# Correct: to+data format → ~53k ✅
curl -s -X POST https://rpc.moderato.tempo.xyz \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"eth_estimateGas","params":[{"type":"0x45","from":"0xa522504eebb35e9e1dbd02ffd37dffdb24afec3b","to":"0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000002","data":"0xa9059cbb0000000000000000000000003e144273d5e4a115c80d46b84d0c5eedbc361a4a00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000f4240","nonce":"0x0","nonceKey":"0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff","validBefore":"0x69b9b005","feeToken":"0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000002"}],"id":1}' | jq .

# Inflated: calls format → ~309k ❌
curl -s -X POST https://rpc.moderato.tempo.xyz \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"eth_estimateGas","params":[{"type":"0x45","from":"0xa522504eebb35e9e1dbd02ffd37dffdb24afec3b","calls":[{"to":"0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000002","data":"0xa9059cbb0000000000000000000000003e144273d5e4a115c80d46b84d0c5eedbc361a4a00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000f4240","value":"0x0"}],"nonce":"0x0","nonceKey":"0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff","validBefore":"0x69b9b005","feeToken":"0x20c0000000000000000000000000000000000002"}],"id":1}' | jq .
```

## Root Cause

In `crates/revm/src/handler.rs:739`:

```rust
if !nonce_key.is_zero() && tx.kind().is_create() && caller_account.nonce() == 0 {
    evm.initial_gas += cfg.gas_params().get(GasId::new_account_cost()); // +250,000
}
```

When `calls` format is used, `inner.to` is `None` (viem clears `to`/`data` and wraps them in a `calls` array). This makes `tx.kind()` return `Create`. Combined with expiring nonce (`nonce = 0`), this incorrectly triggers +250,000 gas (`new_account_cost`) even though the actual calls in `aa_calls` are all CALLs, not contract deployments.

When `to`+`data` is sent directly, `inner.to` is set, so `tx.kind()` returns `Call` and the check is correctly skipped.

## Impact

- Every Tempo TX gas estimate from viem/wagmi is ~6x too high for TIP-20 transfers
- TIP-1010 targets ~50k gas / $0.001 per transfer, but wallets show ~$0.006
- Affects max-send calculations (users cannot send their full balance)

## Suggested Fix

For AA transactions, this check should inspect `aa_calls` instead of `tx.kind()` from the inner TxEnv — `tx.kind()` is meaningless for AA batch transactions since `execute_multi_call` overrides it per-call anyway.

## Workaround

Call `eth_estimateGas` with `to`+`data` format directly, bypassing viem's formatter which converts to `calls`.

payload.body:
When caught up to the tip, the 1s minimum retry in `read_validator_config_with_retry` (`crates/commonware-node/src/validators.rs:41`) causes unnecessary delays for validators. A block that arrives 37ms after the first attempt still costs a full 1s wait, which can cause view-2 proposers to miss their slot.

The 1s floor exists to avoid spamming during historical sync — that is still valid. But near the tip we should poll much more aggressively.

## Proposals

1. **Use `is_syncing` to pick the interval.** The node already calls `node.network.is_syncing()` in the retry log. Use it to branch:
   - Syncing → keep current backoff (`1s * attempt`, capped at 30s`)
   - At tip → poll at ~50ms, no exponential backoff (block is imminent)

2. **Subscribe to new-block notifications instead of polling.** When at tip, `tokio::select!` over a new-block channel + a safety timeout (~500ms). This gets the read within one event-loop tick of the block landing and eliminates busy-wait entirely.

3. **Hybrid.** Start with a short poll (50ms) and double on each attempt up to 1s while syncing, but cap at 50–100ms when at tip. Simple and no new plumbing.

Option 1 is the smallest change. Option 2 is the cleanest long-term but requires threading a block notification channel into the retry loop.

### Describe the bug

## Affected Component
TIP-20 Token Precompile (`crates/precompiles/src/tip20/mod.rs`)

## Description
The TIP-20 token precompile detects overflow/underflow conditions in critical operations (mint, transfer, burn) but does not provide sufficient logging information when these errors occur. This makes debugging overflow scenarios extremely difficult in production environments.

When an overflow is detected, the precompile returns a generic `PanicKind::UnderOverflow` error without logging:
- Which operation failed (mint/transfer/burn)
- Which account was involved
- Current balance/supply values
- The amount that caused the overflow
- Supply cap constraints

## Root Cause
The overflow detection uses `ok_or(TempoPrecompileError::under_overflow())` which creates the error inline without context:

```rust
// BEFORE (insufficient logging)
let new_supply = total_supply
    .checked_add(amount)
    .ok_or(TempoPrecompileError::under_overflow())?;
```

This should be replaced with `ok_or_else(|| { ... })` to enable logging at the error site:

```rust
// AFTER (with detailed logging)
let new_supply = total_supply
    .checked_add(amount)
    .ok_or_else(|| {
        tracing::error!(
            total_supply = %total_supply,
            amount = %amount,
            supply_cap = %self.supply_cap(),
            "TIP20 mint: total supply overflow detected"
        );
        TempoPrecompileError::under_overflow()
    })?;
```

## Affected Operations

1. **Mint - Total Supply Overflow**: When `total_supply + amount` exceeds u128::MAX or supply_cap
2. **Mint - Balance Overflow**: When `recipient_balance + amount` would overflow
3. **Transfer - Sender Underflow**: When `sender_balance < amount` (insufficient balance)
4. **Transfer - Recipient Overflow**: When `recipient_balance + amount` would overflow
5. **Burn - Opted-in Supply Underflow**: When opted-in supply accounting underflows
6. **Fee Refund - Opted-in Supply Overflow**: When opted-in supply accounting overflows during refund


### Steps to reproduce

### Scenario 1: Mint Total Supply Overflow

1. Deploy a TIP-20 token with a supply cap set to a specific value
2. Mint tokens up to the supply cap
3. Attempt to mint additional tokens that would exceed the cap
4. Observe that the transaction reverts with `PanicKind::UnderOverflow`
5. Check logs - no detailed information about:
   - Current total supply
   - Amount being minted
   - Supply cap value

**Expected**: Logs showing the exact values that caused overflow
**Actual**: Generic error with no diagnostic information

### Scenario 2: Mint Balance Overflow

1. Create a TIP-20 token
2. Mint `u128::MAX` tokens to an address
3. Attempt to mint additional tokens to the same address
4. Transaction reverts with overflow
5. No logs indicate which address or what balance/amount values were involved

### Describe the bug

## Bug Description
The DKG (Distributed Key Generation) manager implementation in the Tempo node contained several instances of unsafe `.expect()` and `.unwrap()` calls when interacting with persistent storage journals. Specifically, in `crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/manager/actor/state.rs`, the code assumed that journals would always contain at least one entry after initialization or before pruning.

The primary instance at line 578 was protected by an `if states.size() == 0` check that populated the journal. However, relying on `.expect()` for state transitions in a consensus engine is considered poor practice as it lacks graceful error handling or recovery paths.

## How to Fix
The dangerous calls were replaced with safe error handling using `eyre::Result` and the `?` operator. This ensures that if an invariant is violated, the node logs a descriptive error and shuts down gracefully instead of panicing.

### Files to be modified:
1.  `crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/manager/actor/state.rs`
2.  `crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/manager/actor/mod.rs`

### Detailed Changes:
- **Refactored `Round::from_state`**: Changed signature from returning `Self` to `eyre::Result<Self>` to handle initialization failures safely.
- **Improved Pruning Logic**: Replaced `.expect()` with `.ok_or_eyre()` when calculating segments to prune.
- **Safer Initialization**: Replaced `.expect()` during journal initialization and initial state recovery with proper error wrapping.
- **Updated Call Sites**: Adjusted `Actor::run_dkg_loop` in `mod.rs` to handle the new `Result` return type when initializing a DKG round.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Examine the Code: Navigate to crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/manager/actor/state.rs.
2. Locate Invariants: Search for .expect() calls in the Storage::init and Prune functions.
3. Trigger Scenario (Theoretical):
 - Interrupt the node during its first initialization after the states.append() call but before the states.sync() or subsequent states.read() calls.
 - Manually corrupt the journal files in the node's storage directory (e.g., /tmp/consensus) such that states.size() returns a value greater than 0 but the last entry is missing or unreadable.
 - Start the node.
4. Observation: The node hits the .expect() call at line 578 (in the original version) when attempting to read the current state from an inconsistent journal, resulting in an immediate thread panic and node crash.

### Describe the bug

## Summary
a critical denial-of-service vulnerability where malicious AA 2D transactions with invalid `nonce_key_slot` could crash validator nodes by causing a panic during transaction validation.

### Vulnerable Code
transaction validation used `.unwrap()` on `nonce_key_slot()` which would panic if the value was `None`.
```rust
// crates/transaction-pool/src/validator.rs
state_nonce = match state_provider.storage(
    NONCE_PRECOMPILE_ADDRESS,
    transaction.transaction().nonce_key_slot().unwrap().into(),
) {
    Ok(nonce) => nonce.unwrap_or_default().saturating_to(),
    // ...
};
```

### Impact
- **Denial of Service**: Malformed transactions crash nodes
- **Network Fragmentation**: Repeated crashes reduce validator set
- **No Graceful Degradation**: Node panic is unrecoverable
- **User Experience**: Failed transactions, network disruption

### How to fix
Replaced `.unwrap()` with proper error handling using `.ok_or()`:

```rust
// crates/transaction-pool/src/validator.rs
let nonce_slot = transaction.transaction().nonce_key_slot().ok_or(
    InvalidTransactionError::TxTypeNotSupported,
)?;
state_nonce = match state_provider.storage(
    NONCE_PRECOMPILE_ADDRESS,
    nonce_slot.into(),
) {
    Ok(nonce) => nonce.unwrap_or_default().saturating_to(),
    // ...
};
```

### Changes Made
1. **`crates/transaction-pool/src/transaction.rs`**:
   - Made `nonce_key_slot` field `pub(crate)` for test access
   - Made `tx_env` field `pub(crate)` for test access

2. **`crates/transaction-pool/src/validator.rs`**:
   - Replaced `.unwrap()` with `.ok_or(InvalidTransactionError::TxTypeNotSupported)?`
   - Returns proper error instead of panicking
   - Transaction is rejected gracefully

3. **Test coverage**:
   - Added `test_aa_missing_nonce_key_slot_rejected()` regression test
   - Test simulates the exact bug scenario
   - Verifies transaction is rejected (not crashed)

### Steps to reproduce

1. Initialize a Tempo Node: Run a Tempo node locally (or a mock environment) using the TempoTransactionValidator.   
2. Craft a 2D Nonce Transaction: Create an Account Abstraction (AA) transaction envelope. Set a non-zero nonce_key
 (e.g., 1). This signals to the validator that it should use the 2D nonce validation logic rather than the standard sequential nonce.
3. Simulate an Inconsistent State: The bug specifically occurs when transaction.transaction().nonce_key_slot() returns None. In a live environment, this could happen if the transaction object was partially recovered or if the pool's internal caching mechanism failed to populate the slot during ingestion.
> _For testing: Manually construct a TempoPooledTransaction and ensure its nonce_key_slot OnceLock is set to None._
4. Submit the Transaction for Validation: Submit this transaction to the validator by calling 
validate_transaction.
5. Trigger the Panic Path: The validator enters the 2D nonce validation block. It encounters the following (vulnerable) line:

### Describe the bug

The `tempo download` subcommand does not implement an **exclusive directory lock** (such as a `.lock` file or a standard `flock` check) on the data directory. Currently, it is possible to initiate a snapshot download and extraction while a `tempo` node is actively running and mapped to the same `--datadir`.

This creates a high-priority risk of concurrent writes to the same data directory while files are being held open by the main RPC/Validator process. This results in immediate I/O contention and silent database corruption of the existing chain state.

I recommend implementing a process lock check on the data directory within the download subcommand to align with industry safety standards.

docker run --rm -v /root/tempo-data:/root/.tempo \
ghcr.io/tempoxyz/tempo:latest download \
--chain moderato --datadir /root/.tempo

payload.author: legion2002
payload.body:
## Summary

The `recover_signer` function in `TempoSignature` has a critical design footgun where callers may incorrectly assume a recovered signer address from a keychain signature is fully authorized, when in reality additional validation against the keychain precompile is required.

## Problem

When `recover_signer` is called on a `TempoSignature::Keychain` variant:
1. It validates the inner signature cryptographically
2. It returns the cached access key address from the `KeychainSignature`
3. **It does NOT verify that the access key is actually authorized in the keychain precompile**

This creates a dangerous assumption gap - the function successfully returns an address, implying the signature is valid, but the caller must also separately verify the access key is authorized for the account.

## Location

`crates/primitives/src/transaction/tt_signature.rs` - `recover_signer` function

## Impact

Anyone using `recover_signer` without understanding this limitation could:
- Accept signatures from unauthorized access keys
- Allow critical operations (like EIP-7702 delegation) by spoofed keychain signatures
- Create security vulnerabilities where an attacker signs with their own key but claims to act on behalf of a victim's address

## Root Cause

The `recover_signer` function cannot access the keychain precompile to verify authorization because:
- It's a pure cryptographic function operating on primitives
- It has no access to blockchain state or precompile execution context

## Current Mitigation

PR #1990 adds:
1. A comment warning about this footgun in the `recover_signer` function
2. Explicit skipping of keychain signatures in EIP-7702 authorization list processing

## Required Action

All usages of `recover_signer` must be audited to ensure:
1. Keychain signature cases are handled appropriately
2. Access key authorization is verified separately when needed
3. Critical operations reject keychain signatures if precompile validation isn't performed

## Recommended Fix
We don't have a recommended fix for this yet.

Extending foundry to fuzz test protocol features

## Goal

1. Be able to write invariants about how precompiles interact with the revm handler.
2. Once 1 is achieved, be able to extend this infrastructure, to test more things about tempo. Like complete Tempo Tx flow, making sure live tempo block state transitions adhere to the invariants we write in foundry tests.

## Phase 1: Base Cheatcodes

---

### 1\. `vm.executeTransaction(bytes calldata rlpEncodedTx) returns (bytes memory)` (Critical)

Execute any transaction type through the full handler flow using RLP-encoded transaction bytes.

```solidity
function executeTransaction(bytes calldata rlpEncodedTx) external returns (bytes memory);
```

The transaction type is determined from the first byte (EIP-2718 envelope):

| First Byte | Transaction Type |
| -- | -- |
| `0xc0-0xfe` | Legacy (RLP list) |
| `0x01` | EIP-2930 (Access List) |
| `0x02` | EIP-1559 |
| `0x04` | EIP-7702 |
| `0x76` | Tempo AA |

**Usage:**

```solidity
// Execute any transaction from its RLP encoding
bytes memory rlpTx = hex"02f86c0180843b9aca00850c..."; // EIP-1559 tx
vm.executeTransaction(rlpTx);

// Execute Tempo AA transaction
bytes memory tempoTx = hex"76f9012c01..."; // Tempo AA tx (0x76 prefix)
vm.executeTransaction(tempoTx);

// Replay historical transaction from RPC
bytes memory historicalTx = vm.getRawTransaction(txHash);
vm.executeTransaction(historicalTx);
```

**Why needed:** A unified cheatcode that:

* Accepts standard RLP-encoded transactions (same format as `eth_sendRawTransaction`)
* Handles all transaction types through their respective handlers
* Validates signatures based on tx type
* Runs full pre/post execution hooks (fee collection, nonce management)
* Returns execution result and gas used

---

### 2\. Helper Cheatcodes (Nice-to-Have)

| Cheatcode | Purpose |
| -- | -- |
| `vm.getTransactionKey()` | Get current tx's access key from transient storage |
| `vm.signP256(uint256 privateKey, bytes32 digest)` | Sign with P256 key (Foundry has `vm.sign` for secp256k1) |
| `vm.signWebAuthn(uint256 privateKey, bytes32 challenge)` | Sign with WebAuthn wrapper |

*Note: Foundry already provides* `vm.sign()` for secp256k1 and `vm.signP256()` was recently added.

---

## Expected Behaviour

`vm.executeTransaction` should work similarly to **isolate mode** (`forge test --isolate`):

1. State changes are committed after execution
2. Transient storage is reset per transaction
3. Gas accounting matches production behavior
4. Full handler lifecycle runs (fees, nonces, signatures)

---

## Phase 2: Live Chain Invariant Testing

Once base cheatcodes are ready, we want to run invariants against real chain state—replaying historical transactions and fuzzing on top.

### Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Invariant Test Runner                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. Fork chain at block N                                        │
│  2. Replay block N transactions (verify invariants hold)         │
│  3. Advance to block N+1, inject fuzzed txs                      │
│  4. Verify invariants still hold                                 │
│  5. Repeat for configurable depth                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │                    │                    │
         ▼                    ▼                    ▼
   ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐
   │ Block N  │   ──▶  │ Block N+1│   ──▶  │ Block N+2│
   │ (replay) │        │ (fuzzed) │        │ (fuzzed) │
   └──────────┘        └──────────┘        └──────────┘
```

### Existing Foundry Cheatcodes (Reusable)

| Cheatcode | Purpose |
| -- | -- |
| `vm.createSelectFork(rpcUrl, blockNumber)` | Fork chain at specific block |
| `vm.rollFork(blockNumber)` | Roll fork to different block |
| `vm.warp(timestamp)` | Set block timestamp |
| `vm.roll(blockNumb

### Describe the feature

## Summary

Add support for **periodic spending limits** in key authorization, enabling subscription-based access patterns where spending limits automatically reset after a configurable time period.

## Motivation

Currently, `TokenLimit` in key authorization specifies a one-time spending cap that depletes permanently as tokens are spent. This model works well for single-use or capped authorizations, but doesn't support common subscription-based patterns where:

- A service needs recurring access to a fixed amount per billing cycle
- Users want to authorize "up to X tokens per month" without re-authorizing
- dApps implement subscription models (e.g., streaming services, SaaS payments)

**Real-world use cases:**
1. **Subscription services**: Authorize a streaming service to charge 10 USDC/month
2. **Recurring donations**: Allow an NPO to withdraw up to 5 USDC weekly
3. **Payroll systems**: Enable payroll contracts to transfer salaries monthly
4. **Rate-limited APIs**: Authorize API access keys with per-period token budgets

ERC-20 style approvals cannot fulfill these semantics because they lack periodic limit support. Key authorization with periodic limits provides a native solution.

## Proposed Interface Changes

### Extend `TokenLimit` Structure

**Current:**
```rust
pub struct TokenLimit {
    pub token: Address,
    pub limit: U256,
}
```

**Proposed:**
```rust
pub struct TokenLimit {
    pub token: Address,
    pub limit: U256,
    pub period: Option<u64>,  // Period duration in seconds (None = one-time limit)
}
```

### Update Spending Limit Enforcement

Modify `verify_and_update_spending()` to:
1. Check if the limit is periodic
2. If current timestamp >= `period_end`, reset the period_end:
   - Set `period_end = current_timestamp + period`
   - Set `limit = limit_per_period`
3. Verify and deduct from `limit`


## Semantic Behavior

### Period Reset Logic

```
On spending attempt:
  if current_timestamp >= period_end:
      period_end = current_timestamp + period 
      limit = limit_per_period

  if amount > limit:
      revert SpendingLimitExceeded()

  limit -= amount
```

### Interaction with Existing Limits

- Keys can have a mix of one-time and periodic limits for different tokens
- `getRemainingLimit()` returns current remaining (period-aware)
- `updateSpendingLimit()` updates the per-period amount (resets current period)

### Describe the feature

## Problem 
In [get_pooled_transaction_elements](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/transaction-pool/src/tempo_pool.rs#L352-L371), we first build txs via filter_map + collect::<Vec<_>>() and then extend(...) with results from protocol_pool. Because filter_map produces an iterator with an imprecise size_hint, collect can’t pre‑allocate effectively, and the subsequent extend may trigger another reallocation and memcpy.

## Why it matters
- filter_map makes the iterator’s size unknown, so collect often grows Vec incrementally.
- extend may then reallocate and copy existing elements.
- With large tx_hashes, this adds avoidable allocations and memcpy overhead.

## Where 
In [get_pooled_transaction_elements](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/transaction-pool/src/tempo_pool.rs#L352-L371), the AA‑2D branch builds txs via collect, then appends the protocol pool results.

## Suggested direction

- Pre‑allocate using a known upper bound: Vec::with_capacity(tx_hashes.len()).
- Push AA‑2D results directly into txs, then reserve(protocol_txs.len()) (or extend after reserving) before appending protocol‑pool results.

### Describe the feature

## Problem
In [TreeOfDealings::finalize](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/ceremony/tree.rs#L253-L269) we iterate over each dealing and call [arbiter.commitment](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/cryptography/src/bls12381/dkg/arbiter.rs#L111-L117) with `dealing.reveals().to_vec()` (see the call site in the same block), which copies all reveals per dealing. In [verify_dealing](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/ceremony/tree.rs#L281-L320), we repeatedly call `union(&self.namespace, OUTCOME_NAMESPACE)` and `union(&self.namespace, ACK_NAMESPACE)`; [commonware_utils::union](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/utils/src/lib.rs#L131-L136) allocates a new `Vec<u8>` each time, so these allocations repeat inside the per‑dealing and per‑ack loops.

## Why it matters
- Each call to [union](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/utils/src/lib.rs#L131-L136) allocates a new `Vec<u8>` => doing this inside the per‑dealing/per‑ack path adds avoidable heap churn.
- The `to_vec()` in [finalize](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/ceremony/tree.rs#L253-L269) copies all reveals per dealing => this scales with DKG size.
- The changes are straightforward and reduce allocations without changing logic.

## Where
- [TreeOfDealings::finalize](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/ceremony/tree.rs#L253-L269)
- [TreeOfDealings::verify_dealing](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/ceremony/tree.rs#L281-L320)
- [Arbiter::commitment signature](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/cryptography/src/bls12381/dkg/arbiter.rs#L111-L117)

## Suggested direction
- Precompute `outcome_ns` and `ack_ns` once per `finalize` call and pass `&[u8]` into `verify_dealing` to avoid repeated [union](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/utils/src/lib.rs#L131-L136) allocations.
- Add a slice‑based variant of [Arbiter::commitment](https://github.com/commonwarexyz/monorepo/blob/b9740e83dbdacc45acc2dd14fcbaddc2f02e8252/cryptography/src/bls12381/dkg/arbiter.rs#L111-L117) (e.g. `commitment_ref(&[Share])`) so callers can pass `dealing.reveals()` without `to_vec()`.

### Describe the feature


## Problem
In [build_subblock] we snapshot candidate transactions with `transactions.lock().clone()`.
https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/7f34c562086cd5789ba65b3241a880472db86f81/crates/commonware-node/src/subblocks.rs#L698 we snapshot candidate transactions with this . Which clones the entire `IndexMap`, including its [internal buckets/indices](https://github.com/indexmap-rs/indexmap/blob/2.12.1/src/map/core.rs#L24-L35), even though the build step only needs to iterate the current entries. With large candidate sets (up to `MAX_SUBBLOCK_TXS`), this creates avoidable allocations and memcpy pressure on a hot path.

## Why it matters
- Cloning `IndexMap` copies bucket/index structures in addition to keys/values, which is more expensive than a flat snapshot of the data we actually need.
- This path is executed whenever we (re)build a subblock; extra allocations grow with candidate size.
- We can keep the same lock granularity (short lock for snapshot, no lock during EVM execution) while reducing memory work.

## Where
`crates/commonware-node/src/subblocks.rs`  
`build_subblock` around line ~698:
- `let txs = transactions.lock().clone();` (snapshot)
- `for (tx_hash, tx) in txs { ... }`

## Suggested direction
- Replace the `IndexMap::clone()` snapshot with a lightweight `Vec` snapshot:
  - `Vec<(TxHash, Arc<Recovered<TempoTxEnvelope>>)>` via `iter()` + `Arc::clone()`
  - Keep the lock only for snapshot creation, as today.
- Optional: collect invalid `TxHash` values during iteration and remove them in one locked pass to cut repeated lock/unlock churn.
- Keep current semantics: no lock held during `evm.transact_commit`, still allow removal of invalid transactions by hash.

### Describe the feature

## Problem 
Block::read (block.rs, lines ~74-105) calls buf.copy_to_bytes(header.length_with_payload()) to decode a block. This forces an extra allocation/copy of the entire RLP payload even when the underlying Buf is already contiguous. The comment notes we assume the RLP header is in the first chunk() and that we don’t advance the buf cursor, but it doesn’t address the avoidable copy or payload continuity. If Buf is backed by contiguous bytes (common for Bytes/Cursor), we could decode in-place and advance without cloning the payload.

https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/c470dd10710cfcbac0cc5888bb6d4f61a900b8ce/crates/commonware-node/src/consensus/block.rs#L74-L105

## Why it matters
- Large blocks incur a full payload copy and allocation before decoding. 
- Violates the “zero-copy” intent; adds CPU + heap pressure on hot paths.
- Cursor advancement is implicit via copy; a zero-copy variant needs explicit advance to keep the contract clear.

## Where
impl Read for Block::read_cfg (lines ~74-105):[ copy_to_bytes](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/c470dd10710cfcbac0cc5888bb6d4f61a900b8ce/crates/commonware-node/src/consensus/block.rs#L94
)(...) of [header.length_with_payload](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/c470dd10710cfcbac0cc5888bb6d4f61a900b8ce/crates/commonware-node/src/consensus/block.rs#L89
) then [decode.]
https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/c470dd10710cfcbac0cc5888bb6d4f61a900b8ce/crates/commonware-node/src/consensus/block.rs#L74-L105

## Suggested direction
- Add a zero-copy fast path when buf.chunk().len() >= len: decode from &chunk[..len], then buf.advance(len).
- Fallback for non-contiguous buffers: retain the current copy-based path (or aggregate safely) when chunk is shorter than len.
- Make the “payload must be contiguous” expectation explicit if that is a contract; otherwise keep the dual-path for robustness.

ref: `TMPO-25`
severity: `medium`
impacted files: `crates/precompiles/src/stablecoin_exchange/mod.rs`, `crates/precompiles/src/stablecoin_exchange/orderbook.rs`

## Description

The stablecoin exchange's `calculate_quote_amount()` function rounds down when calculating escrow amounts for bid orders, causing users to systematically deposit less quote tokens than required. This creates cumulative protocol losses that compound with trading volume and can lead to insolvency when the exchange cannot fulfil matched orders.

The function calculates: `quote_amount = (amount * price) / PRICE_SCALE` where `PRICE_SCALE = 100,000`. Rust's integer division always rounds down towards zero. When this function is used to calculate escrow amounts for bid order placement, users deposit slightly less quote tokens than the theoretical value of their order.

The vulnerability manifests in two locations where bid orders are placed (`place()` and `place_flip()` functions).

Beyond the primary vulnerability, the codebase contains numerous similar mulDiv operations throughout the settlement logic and cancellation logic. These calculations lack a consistent rounding policy, with some favouring users and others favouring the protocol, creating accounting inconsistencies.

While individual rounding errors are small, the systemic nature creates guaranteed cumulative losses. The vulnerability becomes more severe with multiple partial fills, where each settlement recalculates independently and rounding errors compound.

The impact of this vulnerability is medium as it creates insolvency risk for the protocol. The likelihood is medium as although the rounding error occurs in every bid order, it is less likely that the exchange's reserves are depleted to the point where legitimate trades cannot settle.

## Recommendations

1. Consolidate all mulDiv price conversion operations into two centralised helper functions with explicit rounding control. Create `base_to_quote()` and `quote_to_base()` functions that accept a `RoundingDirection` parameter.

2. Apply consistent rounding rules: bid order escrow should round up (user pays more), settlement calculations for makers should round down (maker receives less), taker settlement should round down (taker receives less), cancellation refunds should round down.

payload.body:
## Summary

@klkvr proposed that we can replace the 64-byte public key (`pub_key_x` + `pub_key_y`) in P256 and WebAuthn signatures with a single 1-byte recovery ID, saving 63 bytes per signature.

## Current Implementation

Currently, P256 signatures in Tempo require the full public key:

```rust
// crates/primitives/src/transaction/tt_signature.rs:55-61
pub struct P256SignatureWithPreHash {
    pub r: B256,          // 32 bytes
    pub s: B256,          // 32 bytes
    pub pub_key_x: B256,  // 32 bytes
    pub pub_key_y: B256,  // 32 bytes
    pub pre_hash: bool,   // 1 byte
}
// Total: 129 bytes (+ 1 byte type identifier = 130 bytes encoded)
```

WebAuthn signatures similarly include the full public key (64 bytes) plus variable-length authenticator data.

## Proposed Change

Replace `pub_key_x` and `pub_key_y` with a single `recovery_id: u8`:

```rust
pub struct P256SignatureWithPreHash {
    pub r: B256,           // 32 bytes
    pub s: B256,           // 32 bytes
    pub recovery_id: u8,   // 1 byte
    pub pre_hash: bool,    // 1 byte
}
// Total: 66 bytes (+ 1 byte type identifier = 67 bytes encoded)
```

**Savings: 63 bytes per P256/WebAuthn signature**

## Technical Background

### How ECDSA Recovery Works

For any ECDSA signature `(r, s)` over a message hash `h`, there are typically 2 possible public keys that could have produced the signature. The recovery ID (0 or 1) disambiguates which public key is the correct one.

The math is identical for secp256k1 and secp256r1 (P256) - only the curve parameters differ:
- secp256k1: `a = 0`, `b = 7` (used by Ethereum)
- secp256r1: `a = -3`, `b = 0x5ac635d8...` (used by WebAuthn/Passkeys)

### Rust Library Support

The [`ecdsa`](https://docs.rs/ecdsa/latest/ecdsa/) crate provides recovery functionality via `VerifyingKey::recover_from_prehash()`:

```rust
use ecdsa::{RecoveryId, VerifyingKey};
use p256::NistP256;

// To recover public key from signature:
let public_key = VerifyingKey::<NistP256>::recover_from_prehash(
    &message_hash,
    &signature,
    recovery_id
)?;
```

### Why WebAuthn Doesn't Include Recovery ID

WebAuthn was designed for traditional web authentication where:
1. The server stores the public key during registration
2. Subsequent authentications verify against the stored key
3. No need to recover the public key from the signature

As noted in [W3C WebAuthn Issue #1928](https://github.com/w3c/webauthn/issues/1928): "The server (RP) stores the public key after registration. There is no need to include it in authentication as the server has everything it needs to validate."

### Computing Recovery ID Client-Side

Since WebAuthn and Web Crypto APIs don't provide the recovery ID, clients must compute it themselves:

```typescript
// Client already knows: publicKey, signature (r, s), messageHash
// Try recovery_id = 0, then 1, see which recovers the known public key

for (const recoveryId of [0, 1]) {
  const recoveredPubKey = ecrecover(messageHash, signature, recoveryId);
  if (recoveredPubKey === publicKey) {
    return recoveryId; // Found it
  }
}
```

This is a deterministic operation that requires at most 2 attempts.

## Tradeoffs

### Advantages

1. **63 bytes savings per signature**
   - P256: 130 bytes -> 67 bytes (48% reduction)
   - WebAuthn: saves 63 bytes from total size
   - Reduces transaction size and storage costs

2. **Technically sound**
   - Recovery is mathematically equivalent to secp256k1
   - Rust `ecdsa` crate supports P256 recovery
   - Same security properties as current approach

3. **Consistent with secp256k1**
   - Ethereum's native secp256k1 uses recovery (65 bytes: r, s, v)
   - Tempo's P256 would follow the same pattern

### Disadvantages

1. **Non-standard for P256 ecosystem**
   - [RIP-7212](https://github.com/ethereum/RIPs/blob/master/RIPS/rip-7212.md) and [EIP-7951](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7951) both require full public key
   - Most P256 implementations pass full public key
   - Quote from RIP-7212: "verification
payload.title: Proposal: Compress P256 Public Key to Recovery ID

## Summary

Add the ability to restrict Access Keys to specific destination addresses, enabling more granular permission scoping.

## Context

Currently, Access Keys support two configuration options:
- **Spending limits** - per-TIP20 token spending amounts
- **Expiry** - Block timestamp when the key becomes invalid

Add an **allowed addresses** list to `authorizeKey()` - restrict the key to only call specific contract addresses.

- **Gaming**: Scope a session key to only interact with a game contract  
- **Subscription services**: Allow a key to only call a specific payment contract

### Describe the change


## Summary
--
Key authorization signatures in the protocol are currently RLP-encoded, which makes them difficult to sign with common wallets like MetaMask. We should migrate key authorization signing to the EIP-712 typed data standard so that wallets can natively sign the payload.
 
## Motivation
- Wallet compatibility: MetaMask and other wallets do not support signing arbitrary RLP payloads, but they already support EIP-712 typed data.
- Developer ergonomics: Using the same EIP-712 flow as other Tempo transactions simplifies integrations and reduces bespoke signing paths.
- User clarity: Typed data provides clear signing prompts, reducing risk of incorrect or opaque approvals.
 
## Proposal
- Define an EIP-712 domain and typed data schema for key authorizations that captures the current RLP fields (including spend limits and permissions).
- Update the keychain/key authorization flow to produce and verify EIP-712 signatures instead of RLP-encoded payloads.
- Ensure backwards compatibility plan is documented (e.g., if RLP signatures should be deprecated or temporarily supported).
- Update developer documentation and examples to reflect the new signing format.
 
## Acceptance Criteria
- Key authorization signatures are generated and verified using EIP-712 typed data.
- Wallets that support EIP-712 (e.g., MetaMask) can sign key authorization payloads without custom flows.
- Documentation includes the new typed data schema and guidance for integrators.
- Tests cover EIP-712 signing and verification for key authorizations.

## Summary

Tempo currently does not expose BLS finalization signatures or consensus proofs via any API, making it impossible to build trustless light clients or cross-chain bridges. This feature request proposes adding a consensus API (similar to Ethereum's Beacon API) to expose finality proofs.

## Motivation

### Use Cases
1. **Cross-chain bridges**: Bridges need cryptographic proof that blocks were finalized by the validator set to trustlessly relay state to other chains
2. **Light clients**: SPV-style clients need to verify finality without running a full consensus node
3. **Block explorers**: Displaying finality status and validator signatures
4. **Audit and verification**: Independent verification of chain finality

### Current Limitation

While Tempo generates BLS threshold signatures for notarization and finalization internally, these signatures are:
- ✅ Created during consensus
- ✅ Verified by validators
- ❌ **Never stored or exposed**
- ❌ **Discarded after verification**

- External observers cannot verify historical finality
- Light clients must trust RPC providers
- Bridges cannot prove finality cryptographically
- `--follow` mode nodes have zero verification

Ethereum solved this with dedicated light client endpoints on the Beacon Chain API:

```bash

GET /eth/v1/beacon/states/{state_id}/finality_checkpoints

# Light client finality update (includes BLS signatures)
GET /eth/v1/beacon/light_client/finality_update

# Light client bootstrap
GET /eth/v1/beacon/light_client/bootstrap/{block_root}

impl Finalized {

}
```

- **In-memory**: Recent N blocks (for active bridges/light clients)
- **Database/Indexer**: Historical proofs (for full verification)

```rust

pub trait TempoConsensusApi {

    async fn get_block_finalization(

### Describe the bug

## Problem

The execution layer does not reliably persist its latest finalized blocks. At the same time, the consensus layer will never forward finalized blocks to the execution layer twice if processing of the finalized block was previously acknowledged.

This means that in certain scenarios, on restart the node can neither propose nor verify, as the execution layer does not have the block available and neither does the consensus layer forward/backfill the block.

## Suggested solution

Suggested by @klkvr:

Compare the results of:

1. `provider.database_provider_ro().last_finalized_block_number()`
2. `provider.last_block_number()`

If `provider.last_block_number() < provider.database_provider_ro().last_finalized_block_number()`, there is a hole which can be plugged by forwarding missing blocks from CL to EL.

`provider.database_provider_ro().last_finalized_block_number()` is written on every FCU if the finalized blocks is known: https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/blob/56e60a3704433a7635a1e27be44cdaa6dc558358/crates/engine/tree/src/tree/mod.rs#L2633

On restart, the application sends an `FCU(finalized_block_hash = network_finalized_tip)`, which means that there are two options:

1. `provider.database_provider_ro().last_finalized_block_number()` returns `None` - the network finalized blocks past the finalized block known by the node. This means, the restart node will receive a future finalized block from its peers and trigger the backfill mechanism.
2. `provider.database_provider_ro().last_finalized_block_number()` returns `Some(height)` - the finalized block was known / present in the database; the network did not advance past `Some(height)`. This means, we can check if there is a gap between `Some(height)` and the return value of `provider.last_block_number()`, backfilling the gaps if necessary.

## Testing

The scenario where finalized blocks are missing can not be reliably triggered. However, with https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/pull/936 the regular backfill tests should no longer be flaky.

The nodes should not be connected on the execution layer to observe failure: https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/a2f05055a3f52054f6bc0702e78fee9e121f88c8/crates/e2e/src/tests/restart.rs#L179

## Background

Note that in most network conditions this will not lead to a problem:

1. if the network keeps proposing (and eventually finalizing) blocks, the application will attempt to fill gaps from CL to EL (implemented in https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/pull/1173)
2. if nodes are connected via execution layer p2p, the gaps will be filled by fetching them from peers.

The edge cases that would cause a network halt are, for example:

1. a single node network restarts;
2. all nodes in the network go down at the same time in a way that all nodes mutually lose the same block (on restart no new blocks will be proposed, gaps will not be filled from finalized blocks, nodes cannot fetch blocks via EL p2p because they all lack the same block);
3. one or more nodes go down such that the active validators drop below quorum and validators are not connected through EL p2p (no blocks will be proposed, blocks cannot be fetched via EL p2p).

Previously, it was thought that `marshal::Mailbox::get_info` with `Info::Latest` addressed this issue. But this returned the network tip (not the latest locally acknowledged finalized block), which triggered a cascade of way too many (and incorrect) backfills. ### Describe the bug

In an edge case, a user’s on-exchange balance can be incorrectly zeroed when a flip order is filled but the user no longer has sufficient balance or approval to fund the subsequent flip order that gets created. 

When a swap triggers the flip order to be filled, the precompile calls calls `place_flip()` which calls `decrement_balance_or_transfer_from()`. This logic zeroes the user’s balance before attempting a `transferFrom`, and if approval was revoked or the wallet balance is too low, that transfer fails and the user is left with a zero balance even though no tokens were transferred. 

Updating the balance only after a successful transfer should prevent this specific issue.

We need good benchmarks for precompiles and opcodes so that we can design sustainable pricing for the chain.

The goal of the benchmarks is to first generate adequate load for specific precompiles and opcodes so that we can measure how long it takes to build and execute blocks under different conditions (high state size for example). This will also allow us to test different pricing rules.

Once we have some benchmarks that would benefit from testing on a larger state, we should create contracts designed to bloat the state in different ways:
 * Create many accounts
 * Create many accounts and use them in TIP20s
 * Create many TIP20s
 * Add lots of DEX orders

Some opcodes will benefit from generating bytecode which tests that specific opcode with minimal overhead from other instructions, this is used in ethereum gas benchmarking. ### Describe the bug

A malicious proposer can create an AA transaction whose inner calls intentionally corrupt the protocol’s fee accounting invariants by abusing the fact that AA inner calls have no gas reservation and therefore may freely mutate fee related state before the protocol’s post-transaction fee settlement in `collect_fees_post_tx`. 

Inside the AA transaction, the validator uses a malicious fee token implementation together with `burn_blocked` mechanics to burn only a portion of the gas fees that were just collected for that transaction. This puts the system in an inconsistent state where the FeeManager’s recorded `collected_fees` value is higher than the actual spendable balance remaining after the partial burn. 

When the system transaction at the end of the block attempts to transfer the full expected fee amount to the validator, the FeeManager does not actually hold that amount anymore due to the earlier partial burn, causing the system transaction to revert.

payload.author: SuperFluffy
payload.body:
### Describe the feature

The [`ValidatorConfig`](https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/27ae99816ee95c7d81c71ec53c5ebf3e95d82097/crates/contracts/src/precompiles/validator_config.rs) has several footguns that need to be addressed, most of them related to `updateValidator` but they all apply equally in a redesign.

The best way is have only one way to update, disable, and add validators:

The contract is append only; if a validator's IP address or public key is to be changed, a `addValidator` call followed by `disableValidator` must be performed. This way there is only one way to change validator information.

This follows commonware's recommendation to avoid operator error: do not allow changing identities, do not maintain 2 identities. Instead, spin up a new node, observe it joining the validator set, remove the old node.

### Changing the signing key / ed25519 public key of an existing validator

To preface: the consensus layer will not and must not change the makeup of an already existing validator set. The order of private bls12381 shares is dictated by the order (numerically ascending) of public keys and changing their order would very likely lead to a complete breakdown of the consensus layer

---

Assume an operator calls `ValidatorConfig::updateValidator` to change only its public key. Then the following scenarios are likely:

1. the operator shuts down its node restarts it with `new pubkey`; then:
     a. it can't participate in consensus because the other nodes don't recognize it as a consensus participants (because of its changed pubkey)
    b. the network is degraded until a successful ceremony leading to a share for the node
    c. all the while the operator does not understand why its validator produces error logs (ideally) or no logs at all (more likely)
2. the operator keeps the node with `old pubkey` and starts the new node with `new pubkey`:
    a. there is a high chance that the validator copies over the state (and hence private key share) of the old node (bad practice)
    b. the operator needs to wait until `old pubkey` has really dropped out of the consensus participants (which in the worst case can take several epochs due to failing DKG)
    c. there are 2 nodes with different public keys, but the same socket addresses. Which one should be dialed? Only one can respond.

### Changing the incoming address of an existing validator

When an operator changes the public address of a validator, it becomes active on the last block of an epoch. At that moment, the other nodes immediately seize all communication with the node because only the last registered socket address for a given public key is considered.

This means that the operator must stand by while the network evolves, and then immediately restart its node on the last epoch to avoid unnecessary downtime (beyond the downtime that restarting a node necessarily entails).

### Adding a node or changing a node with clashing pubkey

No matter what, an operator cannot be permitted to change the pubkey or incoming address to any value that already exists in the smart contract. Otherwise, a malicious operator could easily cause problems with the remaining set (for example, by settings its public key to one of the other validator's pubkeys).

### Toggling active/inactive validators

Depending on which checks we implement for clashing pubkeys and network addresses, we will need to be extra cautious when allowing to reactive disabled validators (for example, `updateValidator` could permit clashing values but only consider active validators; we don't want `changeValidatorStatus` to provide an escape hatch).

### Proving that a validator controls a public key

This is less critical, but it might be useful to have a validator sign the concatenation of its onchain address + network addresses to prove that they indeed control the pubkey they indicate. This is also to protect them from user error.

### Describe the bug

A user can mint a large number of new TIP20 tokens, create tiny reward streams for each, and schedule all of them to end at the same timestamp. When all streams end at once, the system transaction for that block triggers `finalize_streams()`, which must iterate over every pending stream. System transactions run with a fixed 30M gas limit via `system_call_with_caller`, so the traversal can exceed this limit and cause the system transaction to fail. That results in an invalid block and effectively halts the chain.

### Describe the feature

Swap operations can enter an infinite loop when price calculations round down to zero, causing remainingOut to never decrease. 


**Scenario:**
-   currentTick > 0 and remainingOut = 1
-   Calculation: remainingOut * PRICE_SCALE / tickToPrice(currentTick) ≈ 0
-   Result: amount_out_tick = 0, so remaining_out never decreases, causing infinite loop

**Affected code:**
  - Spec: https://github.com/tempoxyz/docs/blob/351399814954ad6b68759d247e04d2d2f801abb2/specs/src/StablecoinExchange.sol#L679-L697
  - Precompile: crates/precompiles/src/stablecoin_exchange/mod.rs:1069-1087 (quote calculation and remaining_out subtraction)

Credit: @samczsun https://tempoxyz.slack.com/archives/C09KCGR4LQ4/p1762895220576359

### Describe the feature

As mentioned in https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/pull/585#discussion_r2516311152

> As discussed, we think there is a straightforward way to help new peers sync with a finalization cert on some boundary and either a proof of the contract state at that point (who will be the current peers) or by putting the info in the extra data field.

### Additional context

To implement this feature, the `PublicOutcome` type defined here needs to be updated with validator ingoing/outgoing addresses/hostnames (i.e. the values read from the `ValidatorConfig` smart contract, `incomingAddress` and `outgoingAddress`):
https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/412186eed881a3e8d99256cd4c90dd3ee733ad83/crates/dkg-onchain-artifacts/src/lib.rs#L102-L106

Right now, the public outcome only contains the identifiers of the participants as determined by the DKG process (in the form of ed25519 public keys to verify their signatures).

We should probably just replace `participants` with this object here: https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/blob/412186eed881a3e8d99256cd4c90dd3ee733ad83/crates/commonware-node/src/dkg/manager/validators.rs#L113

### Sidequests:

Right now we use a bespoke encoding format. It probably makes sense to change this to RLP when writing onchain data.

function transferWithMemo(address to, uint256 amount, bytes32 memo) external;

function transferFrom(address from, address to, uint256 amount) external returns (bool);

function transferFromWithMemo(address from, address to, uint256 amount, bytes32 memo) external returns (bool);
```
